name: Sultanate of Zanzibar
summary: Created when Oman’s empire was split in 1856; its sultans ruled Zanzibar and the Swahili coast, grew cloves with enslaved labour and ran East Africa’s largest slave market until 1873. A British protectorate from 1890, it was overthrown in the 1964 revolution.

knownFor.label: Shortest war
knownFor.note: Anglo-Zanzibar War lasted under an hour.

location.value: Zanzibar, Pemba and the East African coast.

terrain.value: Low coral islands (Unguja and Pemba) with fertile soils in the west, plus a strip of the Swahili mainland coast until the 1880s.

climate.value: Hot and humid tropical climate with two rainy seasons, shaped by the monsoon winds that carried dhows to Arabia and India.

resources.value: Clove plantations (Zanzibar and Pemba grew most of the world’s cloves), coconuts, and ivory brought from the mainland.

disasters.value: The 1872 hurricane destroyed most clove trees and many ships on Unguja; cholera epidemics, notably around 1869–70, killed many people.

population.value: Perhaps 200,000–300,000 on Unguja and Pemba in the late 1800s, a large share of them enslaved; about 300,000 by the 1950s.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Arab, Indian and African settlers; enslaved people from the mainland.

economicBase.value: Clove and coconut plantations worked by enslaved people, the ivory trade, and slave trading until 1873; later cloves and copra.

tradeRoutes.value: Caravans from Bagamoyo inland to Tabora, Lake Tanganyika and beyond brought ivory and captives to the coast; dhows and steamers linked it to Arabia and India.

wealth.value: Great wealth for the sultans, Arab plantation owners and Indian merchants and financiers, while most people were poor or enslaved.

moneyAndTax.value: Customs duties on trade, farmed out to Indian merchants, were the sultan’s main income; Maria Theresa thalers and Indian rupees circulated.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

keyRulers.value: Sultans Majid bin Said (1856–70) and Barghash bin Said (1870–88); later Khalifa bin Harub (1911–60) under British rule.

succession.value: Al Said family; Britain chose some sultans.

institutions.value: The sultan’s court, a customs house run by Indian financiers and Islamic judges (qadis); after 1890 British officials ran the government.

stability.value: Disputed successions (1870, 1896), the British bombardment of 1896, and the revolution of January 1964 that overthrew the sultan.

eliteConflict.value: Tension between the Arab landowning elite and the African majority, which grew into party rivalry in the 1950s–60s and the 1964 revolution.

armyAndTech.value: A small army of Baluchi and other mercenaries and a few armed ships; from 1877 British officer Lloyd Mathews trained a regular force.

majorWars.value: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896, under an hour long and often called the shortest war in history, settled a disputed succession.

territoryChange.value: Lost the mainland to Germany and Britain (1886–90).

alliancesRivals.value: Relied on Britain against rivals such as Germany; Britain forced the closing of the slave market by treaty in 1873 and made Zanzibar a protectorate in 1890.

inventions.value: No major inventions; Sultan Barghash brought in piped water and the electrically lit House of Wonders (1883).

scienceEducation.value: Mostly Qur’anic schools teaching Arabic and Islam; Christian missions opened schools, and government schools grew after 1900.

openness.value: A cosmopolitan trading hub where Arab, Indian, Swahili, European and American merchants did business, with foreign consuls in Zanzibar Town.

communicationTransport.value: Sailing dhows on the monsoon winds, steamships from the 1870s, a telegraph cable to Aden (1879), and caravans inland.

religion.value: Mostly Sunni Islam, while the ruling Omani family followed Ibadi Islam; Hindu and Christian minorities lived in town.

languageWriting.value: Swahili was the everyday language, written in Arabic script and later in Latin letters; Arabic was used at court and in religion.

artsArchitecture.value: Stone Town’s carved wooden doors and coral-stone houses, the House of Wonders (1883), and taarab music, which grew at the sultans’ court.

socialStructure.value: Arab rulers, Indian merchants, African majority, enslaved people.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the sultan and to Islam bound some people together, but divisions of origin, status and slavery ran deep.

dailyLife.value: Townspeople lived in Stone Town’s coral houses or the Ng’ambo quarter; rice, fish, coconut and spices were staple foods.

neighbours.value: The East African mainland (German East Africa, later Tanganyika, and the Kenya coast), with links across the ocean to Oman and India.

ideasReligions.value: Swahili Islamic scholarship and Sufi brotherhoods such as the Qadiriyya spread from Zanzibar to the mainland; Christian missions came from the 1860s.

colonisation.value: A British protectorate from 1890 under the Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty with Germany, until independence in December 1963.

riseSignals.value: Sultan Said bin Sultan died in 1856; his sons split Oman and Zanzibar, a division confirmed by the Canning Award (1861).

peakPeriod.value: Under Barghash (1870–88), when Zanzibar Town was East Africa’s main port and the House of Wonders was built.

outcome.value: Revolution (1964); united with Tanganyika as Tanzania.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
